intro: Préty is a village on the Saône in the Saône-et-Loire, and the tree at its crossroads has been legally protected since 1909. The plane was planted in 1801 on a mound beside the église Notre-Dame, in the place of an old justice elm, and by the account that survives it marked the Concordat that let priests return to France after the Revolution. Reportedly never pruned since, it has grown to 34 metres tall with a crown spreading 36 metres across the junction. Tournus station is three kilometres away.
meta_description: The Platane de Préty: a plane planted in 1801 in place of a justice elm, reportedly never pruned, classified as a natural monument in 1909.
question_meta: Préty's only mapped tree is its plane, planted in 1801 at the crossroads by the church and classified as a natural monument in 1909.
question_answer: Préty's only mapped tree is the Platane de Préty, a plane planted in 1801 on a mound at the crossroads beside the église Notre-Dame, classified as a natural monument on 25 August 1909.
question_context: This plane has been under state protection since 1909 and, by the accounts that survive, under nobody's saw since it was planted. It went into a mound at the crossroads beside the church of Préty in 1801, replacing an orme de justice, the elm under which local justice had once been dispensed, and it was put there to mark the Concordat that let priests return to France after the Revolution. Left alone, a plane does this: 34 metres tall, a trunk 5.7 metres round, and a crown spreading 36 metres across the junction. The regional heritage federation measures the height at 33.5 metres, close enough to be the same tree. Most planes in France have been pollarded back into fists; this one has the shape the species actually grows. France declared it a site classé, a natural monument, on 25 August 1909, decades before most of the country's remarkable trees got any protection at all. It stands in the open at a village crossroads, free and unfenced, about three kilometres from Tournus station on the Paris to Lyon line.

trees.story:
This plane has been under state protection since 1909 and, by the accounts that survive, under nobody's saw since it was planted. It went into a mound at the crossroads beside the church of Préty in 1801, in the place of an orme de justice, the elm under which local justice had once been dispensed. The reason recorded for planting it was the Concordat, the agreement that let priests return to France after the Revolution. A political tree, in other words, put in by a village that wanted the point made in public.

Left alone, a plane does this: 34 metres tall, a trunk 5.7 metres round, and a crown spreading 36 metres across the junction. The regional heritage federation puts the height at 33.5 metres, close enough to be the same tree on a different day. Most planes in France have been pollarded back into knuckles and fists. This one has the shape the species actually grows.

The protection is the odd part. France classified it as a site classé, a natural monument, on 25 August 1909, decades before most of the country's remarkable trees got anything of the kind. Somebody was paying attention early.

It still stands in the open at a village crossroads on the Saône plain, free and unfenced, about three kilometres from Tournus station on the Paris to Lyon line.
